'''Jordan Stuart Ellenberg''' (born October 30, 1971) is an American mathematician who is a professor of mathematics at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.math.wisc.edu/~ellenber/ |title=Jordan S. Ellenberg |work=wisc.edu}}</ref> His research involves [[arithmetic geometry]]. He is also an author of both fiction and non-fiction writing.

== Early life ==
Ellenberg was born in [[Potomac, Maryland]]. He was a [[child prodigy]] who taught himself to read at the age of two by watching ''[[Sesame Street]]''.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1989/06/07/a-sine-of-a-true-genius/a29172c8-d53f-45da-920c-4e2a407ce97e/ |title=A Sine of a True Genius; Md. Youth Wins Major Math Competition: Jordan Ellenberg |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=June 7, 1989 |author=Amy Goldstein |access-date=October 25, 2017}}</ref> His mother discovered his ability one day while she was driving on the [[Interstate 495 (Capital Beltway)|Capital Beltway]] when her toddler informed her, "The sign says '[[Bethesda, Maryland|Bethesda]] is to the right.'" In second grade, he helped his teenage babysitter with her math homework. By fourth grade, he was participating in high school competitions (such as the [[American Regions Mathematics League]]) as a member of the [[Montgomery County, Maryland|Montgomery County]] math team. And by eighth grade, he had started college-level work.

He was part of the [[Johns Hopkins University]] [[Study of Mathematically Precocious Youth]] longitudinal cohort. He scored a perfect 800 on the math portion and a 680 on the verbal portion of the [[SAT-I]] exam at the age of 12.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/the-wrong-way-to-treat-child-geniuses-1401484790 |title=The Wrong Way to Treat Child Geniuses |newspaper=The Wall Street Journal |date=May 30, 2014 |author=Jordan Ellenberg |access-date=December 9, 2014}}</ref> When he was in eighth grade, he took honors calculus classes at the [[University of Maryland]]; when he was a junior at [[Winston Churchill High School (Potomac, Maryland)|Winston Churchill High School]], he earned a perfect score of 1600 on the SAT; and as a high school senior, he placed second in the national [[Westinghouse Science Talent Search]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Westinghouse Honors Three Young Scientists |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1989/01/27/westinghouse-honors-three-young-scientists/0516bf07-d1a3-4188-973d-ba37416b302b/ |access-date=October 25, 2017 |newspaper=Washington Post |author=Peter Baker |date=January 27, 1989}}</ref> He participated in the [[International Mathematical Olympiad]]s three times, winning gold medals in 1987 and 1989 (with perfect scores) and a silver medal in 1988.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.imo-official.org/participant_r.aspx?id=1590 |title=International Mathematical Olympiad: Jordan Ellenberg |publisher=IMO |access-date=April 8, 2010}}</ref> He was also a two-time [[William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition|Putnam fellow]] (1990 and 1992) while at Harvard.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.maa.org/awards/putnam.html?id=1590 |title=William Lowell Putnam Competition: 1938–2008 |publisher=UNL |access-date=October 10, 2008 |archive-date=October 3, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121003173814/http://www.maa.org/awards/putnam.html?id=1590 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Career ==

In 2004, he began teaching at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and is currently the John D. MacArthur Professor of Mathematics, a position he has held since 2015.<ref name="cv">{{cite web |last1=Ellenberg |first1=Jordan S |title=CV |url=https://drive.google.com/file/d/0B9T4A_0EO9-lVlZTZ2pqbXRGRlU/view |publisher=University of Wisconsin–Madison |access-date=January 28, 2018}}</ref> In 2012 he became a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]] and was a plenary speaker at the 2013 [[Joint Mathematics Meetings]] where he spoke on the subject of number theory and algebraic topology, the study of abstract high-dimensional shapes and the relations between them.<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society]. Retrieved December 2, 2012.</ref><ref name="AMS">{{cite web |title=2013 Joint Mathematics Meetings |url=http://jointmathematicsmeetings.org/meetings/national/jmm2013/2141_invited.html |website=American Mathematical Society |publisher=Mathematical Association of American |access-date=28 January 2018}}</ref><ref name="JMM">{{cite speech |title=How to Count with Topology |first=Jordan |last=Ellenberg |event=AMS-MAA Joint Mathematics Meetings |location=San Diego, CA |date=January 11, 2013 |url=https://quomodocumque.files.wordpress.com/2013/01/jmm-2013-plenary-talk.pdf |access-date=28 January 2018}}</ref> He was named a [[Guggenheim Fellowship|Guggenheim Fellow]] in 2015.<ref name="gugg">{{cite web |title=Fellows |url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/jordan-s-ellenberg/ |website=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation |access-date=28 January 2018 |archive-date=29 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221129172104/https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/jordan-s-ellenberg/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> He was elected as one of the six A.D. White Professors-at-Large at Cornell in 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2019/09/six-ad-white-professors-large-elected|title=Six A.D. White Professors-at-Large elected}}</ref>  His research focuses on "the fields of number theory and algebraic geometry."<ref name="about" />

In addition to his research articles, he has authored a novel, ''The Grasshopper King'',<ref>{{cite book |title=The Grasshopper King: Jordan Ellenberg: 9781566891394: Amazon.com: Books |isbn=1566891396 |last1=Ellenberg |first1=Jordan |year=2003 |publisher=Coffee House Press }}</ref> which was a finalist for the 2004 [[Young Lions Fiction Award]];<ref>[http://www.nypl.org/help/about-nypl/awards/young-lions-fiction-award Young Lions Fiction Award]</ref> the "Do the Math" column in [[Slate (magazine)|Slate]];<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.slate.com/articles/life/do_the_math.html |title=Do The Math |work=Slate Magazine}}</ref> two non-fiction books, ''[[How Not to Be Wrong]]''<ref>{{cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kZTKuMBJP7Y |title=How Not to Be Wrong: The Power of Mathematical Thinking |date=June 24, 2015 |work=The Royal Institution/YouTube}}</ref><ref name="Ellenberg2014">{{cite book |author=Jordan Ellenberg |title=How Not to Be Wrong: The Power of Mathematical Thinking |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2k9KAgAAQBAJ |date=May 29, 2014 |publisher=Penguin Publishing Group |isbn=978-0-698-16384-3}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=How Not to Be Wrong: The Power of Mathematical Thinking: Jordan Ellenberg: 0884817006765: Amazon.com: Books |isbn=978-1594205224 |last1=Ellenberg |first1=Jordan |year=2014 |publisher=Penguin Publishing }}</ref> and ''Shape: The Hidden Geometry of Information, Biology, Strategy, Democracy, and Everything Else'' (2022);<ref>[https://www.jordanellenberg.com/book/shape/ Jordan Ellenberg: Shape]</ref> and articles on mathematical topics in many newspapers and general magazines. 

Ellenberg was a mathematics consultant for the 2017 film ''[[Gifted (2017 film)|Gifted]]'', which features a math prodigy as its protagonist;<ref>{{cite news|last=Brown|first=Gretchen|date=April 27, 2017|title=UW-Madison professor part of formula for 'Gifted'|work=[[Wisconsin Public Radio]]|url=https://www.wpr.org/uw-madison-professor-part-formula-gifted|url-status=live|access-date=September 2, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200902195207/https://www.wpr.org/uw-madison-professor-part-formula-gifted|archive-date=September 2, 2020}}</ref> he also made a cameo appearance in the film as a professor lecturing on the [[Partition function (number theory)|partition function]] and [[Ramanujan's congruences]].<ref name = "gifted">{{cite journal|last=Jackson|first=Allyn|date=August 2017|title=Ellenberg in movie 'Gifted'|url=https://www.ams.org/publications/journals/notices/201707/rnoti-p779.pdf|url-status=live|journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]]|volume=64|issue=7|pages=779|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200902193943/https://www.ams.org/publications/journals/notices/201707/rnoti-p779.pdf|archive-date=September 2, 2020|via=[[American Mathematical Society]]}}</ref>

== Personal life ==

Ellenberg lives in [[Madison, Wisconsin]], with his wife and children.<ref name="about">{{cite web |last1=Ellenberg |first1=Jordan |title=About |url=https://www.jordanellenberg.com/about/ |website=Jordan Ellenberg |date=5 March 2014 |access-date=28 January 2018}}</ref> He is the son of statisticians [[Susan S. Ellenberg]] and [[Jonas H. Ellenberg]].<ref name=Nadis2021 />

He maintains a blog called Quomodocumque which means "after whatever fashion" in Latin.<ref name="quo">{{cite web |last1=Ellenberg |first1=Jordan |title=Quomodocumque |url=https://quomodocumque.wordpress.com/2008/05/02/what-does-quomodocumque-mean/ |website=Quomodocumque |date=2 May 2008 |access-date=28 January 2018}}</ref>
